issues.detail: Examples use Node.js-specific tools (Express, BullMQ, Socket.io) and React, but compatibility declares Python 3.9+ support without Python examples or language-agnostic implementation guidance.

scenarios.name: multi-channel-preference-system
scenarios.rationale: Response A implements all rubric requirements: explicit router with adapters, full category system with enforced non-disableable rules for security/transactional types (via canDisable flag and updatePreference validation), and per-type per-channel preferences. Response B implements the infrastructure (channels, preferences, services) but critically fails the non-disableable enforcement—it allows users to fully unsubscribe from security and transactional notifications, violating the core requirement that these types must always send regardless of user preferences.

scenarios.name: gmail-compliant-email-campaigns
scenarios.rationale: Response A correctly implements all three rubric requirements: RFC 8058-compliant headers (List-Unsubscribe-Post: One-Click), a POST endpoint that unsubscribes without login/confirmation, and separate promotional/transactional queuing with different sender domains. Response B fails critical requirements: implements only a GET endpoint (not POST, which RFC 8058 requires), uses incorrect header syntax (One-Click-Unsubscribe instead of One-Click), and has no separate queue/routing for transactional emails—though it provides good NestJS structure and MongoDB schemas.

scenarios.name: retry-delivery-tracking
scenarios.rationale: Response A implements the exact backoff delays specified (email: 1/5/30 min, push: 30s/2min), includes all required state transitions (queued/sent/delivered/read/failed) with proper timestamps, and provides a robust separate DLQ queue. Response B uses generic exponential backoff starting at 5s/2s (not matching spec), lacks 'delivered' and 'read' states (storing only queued/sent/failed/dead-lettered), and treats DLQ as a status flag rather than a separate queue system.
